cringe: The first 4 seconds are essentially the same title card, which feels slow and self-important for a simple food fact.
The caption/product tie-in to RecipeFix feels bolted on and ad-like because the video itself never earns or mentions it.

first_impression: Elegant food-history packaging, but too slow and too thin for a 21-second social video.
problems: The hook is visually tasteful but not scroll-stopping enough; it reads like a museum placard, not a short-form opener.
The same cover/title setup lasts too long before the actual conflict appears.
The pacing drags: many seconds are spent revealing fragments of sentences viewers can already predict.
The story lacks a sharper human/financial conflict: importer versus tax collector is interesting, but it is underplayed.
The food image feels generic and modern, not connected to the 1893 legal/tariff story.
The quote card sequence from 12–16 seconds is too slow and visually quiet.
The final source bar is tiny and feels like legal garnish rather than useful context.
There is no in-video bridge to RecipeFix, so the caption suddenly turns the post into an ad.
Engagement value is low; there is no surprising final twist, question, or save-worthy takeaway beyond the basic trivia.
fixes: Open with the conflict immediately: “In 1893, one man tried to make tomatoes tax-free.”
Cut the intro title card to under 1 second, or animate directly into the tariff table by second 2.
Make the stakes visual: show “Vegetables = 10% tax” versus “Fruit = free” as the core hook.
Use fewer text beats; combine lines so the viewer is not waiting one second per word.
Replace the generic pasta image with a more editorial tomato/import crate/tariff document collage, or make the food photo secondary.
Shorten to 10–14 seconds: hook, tariff rule, lawsuit, court logic, punchline.
Make the final line sharper: “Botany said fruit. The tax code said vegetable.”
If promoting RecipeFix, include a tasteful final 1-second brand card that connects naturally: “However you classify it, cook it better.”
Increase contrast and size on the source line if it matters, or move it to the caption instead.
Add a comment prompt in caption that fits the content: “Would you tax tomatoes as fruit or vegetables?”
